title: Gabor Initialisation with Matched Filter Energy
summary: Giving half of an encoder's spatial filters a directional starting point while preserving each filter's original norm.
body_markdown:
A 3×33\\times3

spatial filter has just nine positions with which to respond to an edge or a change in texture. We can fill them with independent random numbers, as usual. We can also give some filters a pattern to start from, while leaving them free to learn something else.


In Mirage, we use a mixture. Half of the output filters in selected spatial convolutions keep their Gaussian weights. The other half start as Gabor patterns, with positive and negative regions arranged along a direction. Each replacement keeps the norm of the filter that was there before. We change the pattern while preserving its weight energy.


Gabor initialisation has a history in CNNs. For example,[a 2023 study](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics12194072) uses Gabor filters that remain free to change during learning. We'll build up our version from the spatial pattern, then look at what matching the norm means geometrically. That distinction matters because equal-sized weights can still respond very differently to an image.

This keeps the untouched channels bitwise identical to their Gaussian counterparts. Each replaced filter retains its own original norm, up to floating-point rounding. We match the whole output filter across its spatial and input-channel entries, so a large original filter and a small one keep their respective scales.


Selection and template sampling use deterministic streams derived from the seed and the layer path. Separate streams keep the selected channel indices independent of the random draws used to construct the templates. A paired comparison can therefore reuse the original Gaussian tree without changing unrelated weights.

The constant patch we considered earlier is a simple example. The centred Gabor weights cancel, while a particular Gaussian draw usually leaves a nonzero response. Equal norms allow both behaviours.


## Where the initialisation applies


The default scope covers the encoder's first spatial convolution, its depthwise stem convolutions and the depthwise convolutions in its body spatial mixers. Pointwise matrices, attention, detection and mask heads, the OCR reader and HConvGLU parameters keep their own initialisation.


This separates two kinds of structure in Mirage. Gabor patterns organise the initial spatial filters.[HConvGLU](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/hconvglu) restricts the channel-mixing operator throughout inference. A Gabor-initialised convolution can later become any convolution of the same shape. HConvGLU continues to use its fixed Walsh basis and learned bands after learning.


For someone deploying the model, this choice stays out of the way. The checkpoint contains ordinary convolution weights, and the runtime loads them as usual. There is no Gabor pattern to reconstruct and no extra inference operation. The kernel shapes and parameter counts stay the same.


## Checking what we changed


We ran a small numerical check on a 32-output RGB kernel and a 64-channel depthwise kernel, both 3×33\\times3


3


×


3


. Exactly 48 of the 96 output filters changed. The other 48 remained identical. The replaced filters retained their original norms within FP32 rounding and had zero spatial sum within numerical tolerance.


This checks that the implementation changes the directions and preserves the scales as intended. To learn whether that starting point improves recognition or convergence, we need completed comparisons that vary initialisation independently, use the same evaluation conditions and repeat across seeds. The numerical check answers the smaller question it was designed for.


You can follow the resulting image features into the[instance mask head](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/instance-segmentation) and see how the separate[CTC reader](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/ocr-decoding) handles text. The[Mirage article](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/mirage) brings these parts together, with a playground for trying them on your own images.
